title: The Role of Completeness in Probing Symmetry Breaking
authors: Yuya Kusuki, Hiroyasu Tajima, Shion Yamashika
abstract: Completeness is widely recognized in quantum information as an important property of a family of monotones, because it ensures that no information relevant to state conversion is lost. We show that completeness is also physically important in many-body systems: an incomplete measure of symmetry breaking can miss essential features of symmetry-restoration dynamics. We study the logarithmic characteristic function (LCF), also known as the string order parameter, whose full family is complete for exact i.i.d. pure-state conversion under symmetry-preserving operations for finite groups. We introduce a fidelity-based extension of the LCF to mixed states and identify two concrete advantages over entanglement asymmetry (EA). First, for a finite symmetry group $G$, EA is bounded by $\log |G|$ and can approach the same saturated value for different initial states in the thermodynamic limit, making their relaxation curves indistinguishable and preventing the identification of a discrete-symmetry Mpemba effect. By contrast, the LCF can remain extensive, with a coefficient that depends on the initial state and time, and therefore continues to distinguish their relaxation dynamics. Second, different LCF components can exhibit distinct relaxation and crossing behavior, including cases in which EA shows no crossing. We demonstrate these advantages in spin-chain quenches and a single-qubit system under depolarizing noise. We also develop a replica construction for the fidelity-based LCF in quantum field theory and derive analytical results for conformal field theory.
summary: This work establishes that 'completeness' is a vital physical concept for measuring symmetry breaking in quantum many-body systems. The authors propose the fidelity-based Logarithmic Characteristic Function (LCF) as a superior diagnostic tool compared to Entanglement Asymmetry (EA). LCF's component-wise nature allows it to resolve subtle dynamical features, such as the Mpemba effect, that are masked by EA's saturation or averaging properties.
main_problem: The paper investigates the physical importance of 'completeness' in characterizing symmetry-restoration dynamics in many-body systems, arguing that incomplete measures can miss essential physical features.
main_result: The Logarithmic Characteristic Function (LCF), when extended using fidelity, provides a more complete diagnostic tool than Entanglement Asymmetry (EA) because it avoids saturation and averaging effects that obscure dynamics like the Mpemba effect.
method: The authors introduce and analyze the LCF, a generalization of the string order parameter, and compare its properties against EA using resource-theoretic concepts.
model_or_system: The study applies to general many-body systems, including spin-chain quenches (XXZ/XXX), single-qubit systems under noise, and quantum field theories (CFT).
key_observables: Logarithmic Characteristic Function (LCF) components, Entanglement Asymmetry (EA), and the detection of symmetry-restoration phenomena like the Mpemba effect.
important_parameters: Finite symmetry group size |G|, time evolution (quench dynamics), and the thermodynamic limit.
main_assumptions: The completeness of the LCF family is rigorously established only for exact i.i.d. pure-state conversion for finite groups, though its components are shown to be physically relevant for mixed states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates how EA fails to capture the Mpemba effect in both finite group saturation and group averaging scenarios, while the LCF successfully distinguishes these dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the definition of completeness in quantum information to introducing the LCF for mixed states, comparing its advantages over EA in detecting subtle dynamical features in various physical models.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, information-theoretic tool (LCF) to diagnose non-equilibrium dynamics and symmetry restoration in complex quantum many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding thermalization and quench dynamics.
